title: Text editor with undo/redo
scopeHtml:
Scope: command pattern undo/redo stacks, coalescing, locking, collaborative undo note.

Scope: command pattern undo/redo stacks, coalescing, locking, collaborative undo note.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a text editor core with unlimited undo and redo: insert text, delete text, undo, redo.

Clarify:

  • Functional: insert(pos, text), delete(pos, len), undo, redo.
  • Rules: any new edit after an undo discards the redo history (this is how every editor behaves).
  • Out of scope: cursor, selection, rendering, rich text, multi-file.
  • Scale talk: real editors like VS Code use a piece tree (a balanced tree of text pieces) so inserting in a 100 MB file is fast; our StringBuilder is fine for the LLD and we can mention the upgrade.

Worked example. insert "hello"; insert " world" at 5; delete first 6 chars. Text is "world". Undo gives "hello world", undo again gives "hello", redo gives "hello world". Now insert ">" at 0: redo stack is cleared, text is ">hello world", and redo does nothing.

Industry examples. Every editor and Photoshop uses command history. VS Code, IntelliJ and Google Docs group keystrokes into one undo step (coalescing). Google Docs and Figma use operational transforms or CRDTs for collaborative undo, which is much harder.

Everyday analogy. A pencil with an eraser: each stroke you can rub out in reverse order, and drawing something new after rubbing out means you can no longer redraw the old strokes.

Common interview traps.

  • Snapshotting the whole document per edit (works, but O(n) memory per keystroke).
  • Forgetting to clear the redo stack on a new edit.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Document: the text (StringBuilder).
  • Command interface: execute() and undo().
  • InsertCmd, DeleteCmd: each knows how to reverse itself.
  • Editor: owns the document and two stacks (undo, redo).

Decision gravity. Command-per-edit stores just the delta (position and text), so memory is proportional to what you typed. Alternatives: memento (full snapshots) is simpler but costs O(document size) per step; fine for tiny docs. Reversible: yes, behind the Command interface.

Everyday analogy. A diary of changes instead of photocopying the book after every edit.

Common interview traps.

  • DeleteCmd that does not remember what it deleted, so undo cannot restore it.
  • Capturing deleted text in the constructor instead of at execute time (the text may have changed in between).

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+-------------------+       +--------------------+
| Editor            | uses  | <<Command>>        |
| doc: Document     |------>| execute()          |
| undo: Deque<Cmd>  |   *   | undo()             |
| redo: Deque<Cmd>  |       +--------------------+
| run(cmd)          |            ^           ^
| undo()  redo()    |   +-------------+  +-------------+
+-------------------+   | InsertCmd   |  | DeleteCmd   |
        |               | pos, s      |  | pos, len,   |
        v               +-------------+  |   removed   |
+-------------------+                    +-------------+
| Document          |
| text: StringBuilder|
+-------------------+

Common interview traps.

  • Letting commands reach into Editor; they should only touch the Document.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Command: each edit is an object that can apply and reverse itself. It is the textbook use of the pattern. Alternative: Memento (snapshot). Reversible: yes.
  • Two stacks for history: run pushes to undo and clears redo; undo moves undo to redo; redo moves back.
  • Receiver separation: Commands act on Document, so the same commands work for a file, a test double or a GUI view.
  • Extension: Composite command (macro) that groups many into one undo step, e.g. "type a word" or "replace all".

Worked example. Memory: 100,000 keystrokes of one character each, as individual commands, around 100,000 small objects, several MB. With coalescing of consecutive typing into word-sized commands it drops about 5x and users undo a word at a time. Cap history at, say, 1,000 steps by using a bounded deque.

Industry examples. IntelliJ and VS Code coalesce typing; Photoshop caps history states (default 50 in the app preferences, confirm in your version); Git is a command-history system at heart.

Everyday analogy. A recipe with notes "added salt", reversible by "remove that salt".

Common interview traps.

  • Undoing commands in the wrong order.
  • Unbounded history on a long session.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
import java.util.*;

interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); }

class Document { final StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder(); }

class InsertCmd implements Command {
    private final Document d; private final int pos; private final String s;
    InsertCmd(Document d, int pos, String s) { this.d = d; this.pos = pos; this.s = s; }
    public void execute() { d.text.insert(pos, s); }
    public void undo() { d.text.delete(pos, pos + s.length()); }
}
class DeleteCmd implements Command {
    private final Document d; private final int pos, len; private String removed;
    DeleteCmd(Document d, int pos, int len) { this.d = d; this.pos = pos; this.len = len; }
    public void execute() { removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len); d.text.delete(pos, pos + len); }
    public void undo() { d.text.insert(pos, removed); }
}

class Editor {
    final Document doc = new Document();
    private final Deque<Command> undo = new ArrayDeque<>(), redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Command c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); }   // a new edit kills redo
    void undo() { if (undo.isEmpty()) return; Command c = undo.pop(); c.undo(); redo.push(c); }
    void redo() { if (redo.isEmpty()) return; Command c = redo.pop(); c.execute(); undo.push(c); }
    String text() { return doc.text.toString(); }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Editor e = new Editor();
        e.run(new InsertCmd(e.doc, 0, "hello"));
        e.run(new InsertCmd(e.doc, 5, " world"));
        e.run(new DeleteCmd(e.doc, 0, 6));
        System.out.println(e.text());           // world
        e.undo(); System.out.println(e.text()); // hello world
        e.undo(); System.out.println(e.text()); // hello
        e.redo(); System.out.println(e.text()); // hello world
        e.run(new InsertCmd(e.doc, 0, ">"));    // clears redo
        e.redo(); System.out.println(e.text()); // >hello world
        if (!e.text().equals(">hello world")) throw new AssertionError();
    }
}

Kotlin core:

interface Command { fun execute(); fun undo() }

class Doc { val text = StringBuilder() }

class InsertCmd(private val d: Doc, private val pos: Int, private val s: String) : Command {
    override fun execute() { d.text.insert(pos, s) }
    override fun undo() { d.text.delete(pos, pos + s.length) }
}

class DeleteCmd(private val d: Doc, private val pos: Int, private val len: Int) : Command {
    private var removed = ""
    override fun execute() { removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len); d.text.delete(pos, pos + len) }
    override fun undo() { d.text.insert(pos, removed) }
}

class Editor {
    val doc = Doc()
    private val undoStack = ArrayDeque<Command>()
    private val redoStack = ArrayDeque<Command>()
    fun run(c: Command) { c.execute(); undoStack.addLast(c); redoStack.clear() }
    fun undo() { undoStack.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.undo(); redoStack.addLast(it) } }
    fun redo() { redoStack.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.execute(); undoStack.addLast(it) } }
    fun text() = doc.text.toString()
}

Common interview traps.

  • Not validating positions (negative, past the end); the example skips it, a real editor must throw.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main
world
hello world
hello
hello world
>hello world

Test: undo on empty stack does nothing, redo after a new edit does nothing, delete then undo restores, interleaved undo/redo, out-of-range positions.

Common interview traps.

  • Not testing that redo is cleared.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
A single-user editor is usually single-threaded on the UI thread. Concurrency appears when background work edits the document (auto-format, spell-fix) or in collaborative editing.

Thread-safe version for a shared editor. Make every operation on the history and document atomic with one lock, because execute changes the document and the stacks together and they must stay consistent.

class Editor {
    final Document doc = new Document();
    private final Deque<Command> undo = new ArrayDeque<>(), redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    void run(Command c) { lock.lock(); try { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
    void undo() { lock.lock(); try { if (undo.isEmpty()) return; Command c = undo.pop(); c.undo(); redo.push(c); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
    void redo() { lock.lock(); try { if (redo.isEmpty()) return; Command c = redo.pop(); c.execute(); undo.push(c); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
    String text() { lock.lock(); try { return doc.text.toString(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
}

Why one lock and not two: undo touches the document and both stacks as one unit; splitting locks invites an inconsistent state where the text changed but the history did not. Throughput is irrelevant here (human typing speed).

Why multi-user is different (gravity, one-way door). With two people editing, "undo" means undo MY last edit, not the last edit globally, and positions shift as others insert text. Google Docs uses operational transformation and Figma and others use CRDTs, where each edit is transformed against concurrent ones and each user has their own undo stack. Choosing OT or CRDT is a foundational, hard-to-reverse architecture decision.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking only the document but not the stacks.
  • Assuming a global undo stack works for collaboration.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Coalesce consecutive inserts into one command (merge if adjacent and within 500 ms).
  • Macro command for replace-all (Composite).
  • Bounded history (drop the oldest) to cap memory.
  • Cursor and selection restored on undo.
  • Large files: piece table or rope instead of StringBuilder.
  • Save points: mark a clean state to show an "unsaved changes" dot.

Common interview traps.

  • Merging commands that are not adjacent, corrupting positions.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Command pattern: each edit knows how to apply and reverse itself.
  • Two stacks; a new edit clears redo.
  • Delete must remember removed text; store deltas, not snapshots.
  • Bound the history and coalesce typing.
  • One lock for a shared editor; real collaboration needs OT or CRDT with per-user undo.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement undo in a text editor, and what is the difference between the Command and Memento approaches?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard question for the Command pattern; the signal is the cost trade-off, not the name.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With Command, each edit is an object with execute() and undo() that stores just the delta (position and text), so memory is proportional to what the user typed. With Memento, I snapshot the whole document before each edit: simple, but O(document size) per step. I use Command for an editor, and Memento only for tiny state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
InsertCmd(pos, s): execute = insert(pos, s)   undo = delete(pos, pos+len(s))
DeleteCmd(pos, n): execute = remember removed, delete   undo = insert(pos, removed)

DeleteCmd must remember what it deleted, and it must capture that at execute time, not in the constructor, because the text under the range might have changed between creating and running the command. Commands touch only the Document, so the same commands work against a file, a test double or a GUI view.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public void execute() { removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len); d.text.delete(pos, pos + len); }
public void undo()    { d.text.insert(pos, removed); }
override fun execute() { removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len); d.text.delete(pos, pos + len) }
override fun undo()    { d.text.insert(pos, removed) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• DeleteCmd that does not store the removed text.
  • Snapshotting a 10 MB document per keystroke.
  • Commands reaching into Editor instead of only Document.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Memory for 100,000 single-char commands? -> About 100,000 small objects, several MB; coalesce and bound history.
  2. When is Memento right? -> Small state, complex edits that are hard to reverse.
  3. How do you group "replace all" into one undo step? -> A composite (macro) command that undoes its children in reverse order.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE names the pattern. Senior quantifies memory, captures state at execute time, and mentions composite commands and bounded history.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An editor that snapshotted a document per edit ran out of memory on large files.

questions.promptHtml: Why two stacks for undo/redo, and why does a new edit after an undo clear the redo history?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can state the state machine and justify the redo rule rather than memorise it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: run(cmd) executes, pushes on the undo stack and clears redo. undo pops from undo, reverses it, pushes it on redo. redo pops from redo, re-executes it, pushes on undo. A new edit clears redo because the redo commands were recorded against a document state that no longer exists: replaying them on a changed text would corrupt positions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
state                      undo stack     redo stack
type A, type B             [A, B]         []
undo                       [A]            [B]
undo                       []             [A, B]
redo                       [A]            [B]
new edit C                 [A, C]         []     <- B is gone

The commands in redo assume the document is exactly the state after undo. Git is similar: committing on an old checkout creates a branch; editors choose to discard instead (undo trees like Vim's keep branches).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting redo.clear().
  • Undoing in the wrong order.
  • Unbounded history over a long session.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you bound memory? -> Bounded deque dropping the oldest step (for example 1,000).
  2. What if undo is called on empty? -> No-op, not an exception.
  3. How would you keep branches (undo tree)? -> Nodes with parent and children, current pointer; redo picks the latest branch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites the stack moves. Senior explains the invariant (redo valid only for the current state) and knows undo trees as the alternative.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A redo bug applied stale commands after a paste and produced garbled documents for a few users.

questions.contextHtml:
QA reports: "Undo of delete sometimes restores the wrong text after I edit above it", and "after undo, redo reapplies the delete to the wrong range". Code:

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class DeleteCmd implements Command {
    private final Document d; private final int pos, len; private final String removed;
    DeleteCmd(Document d, int pos, int len) {
        this.d = d; this.pos = pos; this.len = len;
        this.removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len);   // captured at construction
    }
    public void execute() { d.text.delete(pos, pos + len); }
    public void undo()    { d.text.insert(pos, removed); }
}
// Editor
void run(Command c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); }          // redo not cleared
class DeleteCmd(private val d: Doc, private val pos: Int, private val len: Int) : Command {
    private val removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len)   // captured at construction
    override fun execute() { d.text.delete(pos, pos + len) }
    override fun undo()    { d.text.insert(pos, removed) }
}
fun run(c: Command) { c.execute(); undoStack.addLast(c) }    // redo not cleared

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixes one and leaves the other, or says the commands are "fine" because the happy path passes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are commands ever created ahead of time (queued, recorded as macros)? Is the document mutated by anything other than commands?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Capture state in execute(), clear redo in run.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) removed captured at construction: if the command is created, then another edit changes the text, then the command executes, removed is stale and undo restores wrong text; (b) run does not clear redo, so a stale redo command applies to a changed document (the wrong range); (c) no bounds validation of pos/len.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test: build DeleteCmd, run an insert first, then execute and undo, and compare to the original text. Test: undo, new edit, redo must be a no-op.
  5. Root cause: The command holds a snapshot of state from the wrong moment, and the redo history is not invalidated.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
private String removed;
public void execute() {
    if (pos < 0 || pos + len > d.text.length()) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException();
    removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len); d.text.delete(pos, pos + len);
}
void run(Command c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); }
private var removed = ""
override fun execute() {
    require(pos >= 0 && pos + len <= d.text.length)
    removed = d.text.substring(pos, pos + len); d.text.delete(pos, pos + len)
}
fun run(c: Command) { c.execute(); undoStack.addLast(c); redoStack.clear() }
  1. Prevention: Tests for interleaved undo/redo and for "redo after new edit does nothing"; property test: random edits then undo all must equal the original text.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not snapshot the whole document to dodge the capture bug. The "undo everything returns the original" property test is cheap and catches most mistakes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Command executed twice by redo? -> execute re-captures removed, which is correct because the document is in the same state.
  • Undo after the document was saved? -> Save point marks a clean state index; undo can move away from it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A macro recorder that built commands ahead of time restored stale text on undo until state capture moved to execute time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixes one defect.
  • Hire: both defects, with tests.
  • Strong hire: bounds validation, property test, explains why capture time matters.

questions.contextHtml: Users complain: undoing a 2,000-word paragraph takes 11,000 Ctrl+Z presses because each character is a command. Also "Replace all" (340 occurrences) must be one undo step. Memory profile after a 4-hour session shows 1.4M command objects.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Merges all consecutive commands regardless of position or timing, or stores snapshots for macros.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What defines "one typing burst" (pause 500 ms, whitespace, cursor jump)? Should a delete merge with inserts? Max history size?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the history at 1,000 entries with a bounded deque.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: merge in Editor.run; ask the previous command to absorb the new one (mergeWith); record raw chars and group at undo time.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test: typing "hey" yields one command; typing at a different position does not merge; replace-all undo restores the original text in one step.
  5. Root cause: One command per keystroke is the right unit of execution but the wrong unit of undo.
  6. Fix: Add boolean mergeWith(Command next) to the interface. InsertCmd merges when next is an insert at exactly pos + s.length() and within 500 ms (clock injected). Editor.run calls top.mergeWith(c); if true, execute c but do not push a new entry. Replace all becomes a CompositeCmd of children: execute runs in order, undo runs in reverse order.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean mergeWith(Command c) {
    if (c instanceof InsertCmd n && n.pos == pos + s.length() && n.at - at < 500) { s += n.s; return true; }
    return false;
}
fun mergeWith(c: Command): Boolean {
    if (c is InsertCmd && c.pos == pos + s.length && c.at - at < 500) { s += c.s; return true }
    return false
}
  1. Prevention: Merge-boundary tests (non-adjacent, long pause, newline), and a test that merged undo equals unmerged state.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Merging commands that are not adjacent corrupts positions. Coalescing makes undo coarser; I'd break a burst at whitespace/punctuation to feel natural. I would not drop the per-keystroke execution; only history is coalesced.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should a cursor move break a burst? -> Yes; make cursor movement a boundary.
  • Composite command partially fails midway? -> Undo the children already applied, then rethrow, so the document stays consistent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "replace all" without composite grouping made users press undo 400 times; support dubbed it "the undo tax".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: merges everything.
  • Hire: adjacency/time-based merge, composite for macros.
  • Strong hire: boundary rules, failure atomicity in composite, bounded history.

questions.contextHtml: The editor has a UI layer calling Editor methods. Current tests drive a headless browser and take 3 minutes; they missed a bug where undo on an empty stack throws. You are asked to propose a test plan that runs in under a second.
questions.promptHtml: What do you test and how does the design make it possible?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: More UI tests, or only the happy path undo.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does Editor depend on any UI class? Where does position validation live?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the empty-stack regression test.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Failures come from: empty stacks, redo after new edit, restore of deleted text, out-of-range positions, interleaving of undo/redo.
  4. How I'd verify each: Pure unit tests against Editor and Document (no UI): commands only touch Document, so no mocks are needed.
  5. Root cause: The design is testable because of receiver separation; the slow suite tests the wrong layer.
  6. Fix: Table of tests plus a property test:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Editor e = new Editor();
e.run(new InsertCmd(e.doc, 0, "hello"));
e.run(new InsertCmd(e.doc, 5, " world"));
e.undo(); e.undo(); e.undo();                  // third undo on empty stack: no exception
assert e.text().isEmpty();
e.redo(); e.redo(); assert e.text().equals("hello world");
e.run(new InsertCmd(e.doc, 0, ">")); e.redo(); // redo cleared
assert e.text().equals(">hello world");
val e = Editor()
e.run(InsertCmd(e.doc, 0, "hello"))
e.run(InsertCmd(e.doc, 5, " world"))
repeat(3) { e.undo() }                           // third undo on empty stack: no exception
check(e.text().isEmpty())
e.redo(); e.redo(); check(e.text() == "hello world")
e.run(InsertCmd(e.doc, 0, ">")); e.redo()        // redo cleared
check(e.text() == ">hello world")
  1. Prevention: Property test with a seeded random sequence of inserts, deletes, undos and redos: after undoing everything the text equals the original; after redoing everything it equals the final text. Also out-of-range positions must throw and leave state unchanged.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keep a handful of UI smoke tests only. I would not mock Document; the real StringBuilder version is faster than a mock and checks real behaviour.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Test the concurrent editor? -> Many threads running commands, then assert undo-all returns to the initial text and stacks are consistent.
  • Test coalescing? -> Inject the clock and assert merges at 499 ms and not at 501 ms.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A seeded random undo/redo property test found a composite-command ordering bug in 40 seconds that manual QA had missed for a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: UI-only tests.
  • Hire: unit tests on empty stack, redo clear, restore.
  • Strong hire: property test with seed, clock injection for merging, failure-state checks.

questions.contextHtml: A spell-fix service edits the document on a background thread while the user types. Symptoms: occasionally StringIndexOutOfBoundsException in InsertCmd.undo, an undo that deletes the wrong characters, and once the undo stack contained a command that was also in the redo stack. Both threads call editor.run(...). Current code has no locking; a teammate suggests making only Document.text a synchronized method.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the races and design the fix, including what undo should mean when a background edit sits between two user edits.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Synchronizes document methods only and calls it done.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should background fixes be undoable by the user? Do commands carry absolute or relative positions? Does the UI render from the same document?
  2. Immediate mitigation: One lock around every Editor operation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) run mutates the document and two stacks as one unit; interleaving leaves them inconsistent (command in both stacks); (b) ArrayDeque is not thread-safe; (c) positions: the background edit shifts text so the user's undo hits the wrong range; (d) locking only the document does not protect the stacks.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stress test: two threads applying random commands with all undos at the end must restore the original text; check stack sizes.
  5. Root cause: The unit of consistency is document plus history, but they are protected separately (or not at all). Absolute positions go stale when others edit.
  6. Fix: One ReentrantLock guards run, undo, redo and text(). For the position problem: background edits are recorded in the same history as ordinary commands (so undo order is the real order), or tagged as non-undoable "system" edits that shift the positions of earlier commands (operational-transform-lite).
Languages: Java · Kotlin
void run(Command c) { lock.lock(); try { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }
void undo() {
    lock.lock();
    try { if (undo.isEmpty()) return; Command c = undo.pop(); c.undo(); redo.push(c); }
    finally { lock.unlock(); }
}
fun run(c: Command) = lock.withLock { c.execute(); undoStack.addLast(c); redoStack.clear() }
fun undo() = lock.withLock {
    undoStack.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.undo(); redoStack.addLast(it) }
}
  1. Prevention: The stress test; documentation of the invariant "document and both stacks change together"; a code rule that no command is executed outside Editor.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One lock, not two: splitting invites a state where text changed but history did not. Throughput is irrelevant at human typing speed. I would not make undo silently skip commands it cannot apply; failing loudly is better.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• UI renders while the lock is held by a long background command? -> Keep background commands small and chunked, or take snapshots for render.
  • Why ReentrantLock over synchronized? -> Either works; a lock enables tryLock timeouts and fairness if needed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An auto-formatter edited the buffer on a worker thread; occasional undo corruption took weeks to reproduce until a lock covered document and history together.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: document-only synchronization.
  • Hire: single lock over document and stacks.
  • Strong hire: addresses position shifting and the meaning of undo for background edits.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants Google-Docs-like multi-user editing for 2-20 people in one document. The prototype shares the single undo stack across users via the server. Bug reports: "Undo removed my colleague's paragraph", "my undo does nothing after Ben typed above", and positions drift after concurrent inserts.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the shared-stack design fail and what do you choose instead?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a lock so only one person edits at a time", or "add a global undo permission".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Offline editing needed? Server authoritative or peer-to-peer? Rich text or plain? Expected latency? Maximum document size and active editors?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make undo per user: undo my last edit only, not the last edit globally.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) global stack means "last edit" belongs to whoever typed last; (b) positions are absolute, so a concurrent insert shifts everything behind it; (c) the inverse of an old command depends on edits made since.
  4. How I'd verify each: Simulate two clients with interleaved edits and check both converge and undo only affects the owner's text.
  5. Root cause: Absolute positions plus a single history assume a single author. Concurrent edits must be transformed against each other.
  6. Fix: Pick a convergence model. Operational transformation (OT, Google Docs style): server orders operations and transforms concurrent ones against each other, and each user's undo is the inverse of their own operation transformed by everything since. CRDTs (Figma and others use variants): each character has a unique id and ordering rule, merges are commutative, and each user keeps a local undo stack of their own operations. I would pick a CRDT library for offline support rather than hand-roll either (verify maturity for the chosen language).
  7. Prevention: Fuzz tests: random concurrent edits on N clients must converge to identical text; property tests for undo of own edits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: OT needs a central server and a hard-to-get-right transform function; CRDTs cost metadata per character and larger documents. This choice is a foundational, hard-to-reverse architecture decision, so I would prototype with fuzzing before committing. I would not hand-write the algorithm for production.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Undo of an edit another user has since modified? -> The inverse operation transforms against later operations and may become a no-op or partial; define the intended outcome in the product spec.
  • Local-first single user? -> The simple command stack is enough; collaboration is a different system.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared-stack prototype demoed fine with two people typing at different times and fell apart in the first meeting when both typed at once.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single editor lock or shared stack.
  • Hire: per-user undo and names OT or CRDT.
  • Strong hire: compares OT and CRDT trade-offs, proposes fuzz-based convergence testing, flags it as a one-way door.

questions.contextHtml: The editor must open a 200 MB log file. With StringBuilder, inserting at the start of the file takes 90 ms (copying 200 MB of chars is about 400 MB in memory for UTF-16, verify for your JVM's compact strings) and typing lags. Undo history: users replace-all on the whole file, and a DeleteCmd stores the removed text; one replace-all stored 180 MB of removed text, and ten of them exhausted a 4 GB heap.
questions.promptHtml: Fix the text storage and the history memory.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the heap" or compress the whole file on each edit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it plain text with random access edits? Are edits mostly near the cursor? Must history survive restart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Bound history by bytes, not just count, and refuse to keep full removed text above a cap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) StringBuilder.insert is O(n) per edit (array shift); (b) DeleteCmd stores removed text, so history memory is proportional to deleted bytes times number of steps; (c) a replace-all is stored as copies of both old and new text.
  4. How I'd verify each: JFR/allocation profile; time insert(0, ...) at 200 MB; heap histogram showing char[] or byte[] dominating.
  5. Root cause: A contiguous array is the wrong structure for large documents with frequent mid-file edits, and the command stores payloads instead of references.
  6. Fix: Text storage: a piece table or rope (balanced tree of pieces). VS Code uses a piece tree: the original file is immutable, edits go into an append-only buffer, and the document is a sequence of pieces pointing into those buffers; insert and delete are O(log n) and never copy file contents. With a piece table, a delete is just splitting pieces, so the command stores piece references, not text, and undo reuses them: history memory becomes proportional to number of edits, not bytes deleted.
original buffer (200 MB, read only)    add buffer (append only)
pieces: [orig 0..5000][add 0..4][orig 5000..N]
delete = split pieces; undo = restore piece list
  1. Prevention: Benchmarks for edits at start/middle/end of a 200 MB file; history memory metric; cap on total undo bytes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A piece table is more complex than StringBuilder and needs periodic compaction when the piece list fragments; worth it only for large files, and the Command interface stays the same, so I would introduce it behind Document. I would not rewrite undo to snapshots.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Random access by line number? -> Maintain a line index per piece or tree node (line-break counts in the tree).
  • Fragmentation after thousands of edits? -> Merge adjacent pieces or rebuild periodically.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A log viewer's "delete selection" copied the removed range into history; deleting 1 GB files crashed the tab until history stored piece references.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bigger heap.
  • Hire: piece table or rope, history by reference.
  • Strong hire: quantifies copy cost, memory per history step, keeps the Command interface stable, plans compaction.
